implementation_notes: Ruby gives a class only one superclass, so the behavior a layer shares usually travels in a module: include inserts it into the ancestor chain after the class, extend adds it to the singleton class for class-level methods, and ActiveSupport::Concern adds the included/class_methods hooks plus module dependency resolution. The class route is what frameworks generate: Rails' ApplicationRecord < ActiveRecord::Base with self.abstract_class = true is exactly the application's layer supertype, and every model inherits from it. Prefer the module when sharing behavior, an abstract class when the layer must also share state, framework identity or a database connection.
code_sketch:
module Auditable                                  # a slice of layer behavior
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern
  included do
    before_save { self.updated_at = Time.now }
  end
end
class ApplicationRecord < ActiveRecord::Base
  self.abstract_class = true                      # the layer's declared type
end
class User < ApplicationRecord
  include Auditable                               # member gains the behavior
end
pitfalls: include inserts the module below the class in the ancestor chain: a method defined on the class always wins, and with several included modules the last include has precedence - order mistakes are silent.
A concern that assumes the abstract base (columns, callbacks, connection) fails when included into a plain class; ActiveSupport::Concern resolves module dependencies but not framework state.
Reopening a framework base (monkey-patching ActiveRecord::Base) changes every model in the application; extend an application-level abstract class instead.
